competitive_landscape: The lagoon is served today by the state operator LAGFERRY and private operators on a LASWA-regulated network of diesel boats. Demand is proven (the Ikorodu corridor is busy) but the experience is constrained by safety perception, reliability and aging craft. There is no foiling incumbent — and a stable, software-monitored, zero-wake platform that earns public trust is itself the core value proposition.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire core lagoon network — CMS↔Ikorodu (~13 nm), ↔VI/Lekki (~4 nm), ↔Apapa (~4 nm) — sits comfortably inside the 70 nm all-electric envelope with terminal charging, supporting high-frequency mass-commuter and corporate rotations.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta-LR's 700 nm hybrid range covers the long growth corridors — Lekki/VI↔Epe (~30 nm) and CMS↔Badagry (~28 nm) — with no charging-infrastructure dependency at the fast-developing corridor ends.

precedents.why_it_matters: Demonstrates electric foiling as the backbone of inter-island mobility at national scale — the proof that a foiling fleet can be the transport layer, not a novelty.

regulatory_note: The Lagos State Waterways Authority (LASWA) is the primary regulator (terminals, route licensing, safety), with the National Inland Waterways Authority (NIWA) at federal level and the Lagos State Ministry of Transportation for policy. LASWA's existing terminal network and safety regime is a major de-risking factor vs greenfield markets.
seasonality: The sheltered lagoon basin is operable year-round; the binding variables are wet-season squalls (Apr–Oct), water-hyacinth/debris mats and shallow-channel silting. The dry season (Nov–Mar) is calmest. No cyclone exposure — a relatively benign year-round environment.
signature_routes: Lekki/VI ↔ Epe (Free Zone hybrid line-haul, ~30 nm)
summary: Lagos is Africa's largest city (~20–25M people) spread across islands and peninsulas around the vast Lagos Lagoon, with legendary road congestion across a handful of chronically jammed bridges. The state has made water transport a strategic priority for a decade: the Lagos State Waterways Authority (LASWA) regulates an expanding terminal network and operators (LAGFERRY and private fleets) run a growing service from CMS/Marina, Falomo, Ikorodu, Apapa and the Lekki axis. Safety, reliability and aging diesel boats are the binding constraints — exactly where a stable, software-defined, zero-wake foiling-electric platform changes the proposition. This is the flagship emerging-market commuter case: a megacity that wants the water, with a regulator already in place.
tagline: Africa's biggest city, built around a lagoon, with the world's most punishing bridge traffic — a megacity that already wants to move people onto the water and has the regulator to do it.
